title: Defence and Globalisation
author: Modern
content:
DEFENCE AND GLOBALISATION 

By Nicholas Marsh

      

Globalisation is the world's most dynamic economic, political and cultural trend.  It will create the background of the security issues of the next century.  The economic integration of the West was initiated as a Cold War security measure and the future of the UK is tied to the future of the West. 

In the next century we will have to face the security consequences of globalisation.  Great powers like Russia and China have a growing perception of globalisation as a means of ensuring the continuing domination of the US and her allies over world politics and economics.  They have already started, in areas like the Taiwan Straits, to oppose the influence of the US.  Globalisation lies at the heart of the threat felt by these regimes. 

On a local scale, globalisation has forced many to adopt the fundamentals of their culture or religion to defend their way of life from the ubiquitous spread of western culture associated with the advance of globalisation.  National and religious conflicts of identity within states  are the greatest contemporary threat to international peace and stability.  The militant groups behind them are partly driven by a reaction to the process of globalisation. 

Globalisation

Globalisation is the  social, economic and political process through which advances in communications and transport technology have enabled a fast flow of ideas and goods across the world.  International trade has been the motor of this process that started with the great voyages of discovery in the middle ages, and has grown exponentially since the end of the Second World War. 

Globalisation has profoundly affected the world's cultural life.  McDonalds has become ubiquitous, and the same music, fashions, soft drinks and vehicles can be found throughout the world.  Our homes are filled with goods and styles that have been sourced from many different parts of the world.  The human rights agenda and the green movement have put local or regional issues onto the world stage, and highlighted the world's responsibility to end problems like deforestation and political repression.  In all globalisation represents the most profound process of change in the character of both the world and our local environments. 

During the 1980',s globalisation became the worlds most dynamic economic trend. Foreign direct investment and  international intra-firm collaboration doubled,  and by the end of the decade half of all visible imports into OECD states were internationally sourced components and goods used in manufacturing. According to the World Trade Organization, the value of world traded merchandise passed $4,000 billion for the first time last year, and is expected to rise a further 8% this year.  In addition the value of trade in commercial services topped $1,000 billion, a growth of 8% on the previous year. 

The West

Globalisation was created as a security mechanism to strengthen the West during the Cold War.  Economic integration and development were the best ways of securing the alliance and preventing populations from being seduced by communism.  The EEC was developed in the 1950s to bind together the economies of Western Europe, in particular France and Germany, to prevent another war.    The US invested heavily in both Western Europe and Japan to prevent impoverished societies from falling to communism.  Japanese and European entrepreneurs were allowed access to the lucrative US market to encourage economic growth.  The West became a bloc of states that were economically integrated and  united against communism.  Lead by the US  it  comprised  leading democratic and industrial powers, namely Western Europe, North America, Japan and Australasia. 

Trade and economic development were used to counter the communist threat to South-east Asia during the 1960s and '70s.  ASEAN was extended to become a trading bloc in 1976 as a reaction to the fall of  South Vietnam and Cambodia.  Already Taiwan, Singapore and Hong Kong had taken advantage of  strategic US trade policies to promote export lead growth.  While they have not embraced democracy their governments became firm allies of the West and allowed the  free movement of people and goods. 

Political integration closely followed economic ties.  Intergovernmental organisations proliferated as states took measures to manage both their political and economic relations.  Institutions as diverse as NATO, the EEC, OECD, ASEAN and the G7 were instituted in the decades following the Second World War.  These, and many other organisations, created an unprecedented level of  contact between peacetime governments.  This contact helped to reduce uncertainty and so decrease the risk of war between the states opposed to the Warsaw Pact. 

The undeveloped world has been left on the periphery.  It has been unable to take advantage of the liberal trading order and most societies are affected by, rather than participants in the process of globalisation.  With few opportunities to travel, little income to spend on foreign imports and a fraction of the foreign direct investment found in the West, the rest of the world's population has been barred from the processes of globalisation.  As the gap between developed and undeveloped countries grows, the EU and US have become a target for mass immigration. 

Integration and security

The project to integrate the leading democratic and industrial powers has created a new era in international relations. Economic integration makes war between peers practically impossible because  vital war materials like microchips have to be soured from potential enemies. In addition the expected gains from a war must be balanced against the costs of losing trade.  If the opportunity cost of severing trade links is too high then a  war will not be fought for economic gain. 

It is one  of the truisms of international relations that democracies are extremely reluctant to fight each other.  This reluctance is due to the need to acquire the consent of the whole of the population for a risky venture like war, a common interest in peaceful economic development, habits of settling problems diplomatically and close similarities between societies which promote cultural ties.  When economic integration is linked to political ties that remove tension from disputes, such as over  territory or  micro-economic competition, there is very little motivation for war within the West. 

It is the structure of international trade rather than the amount that has had the most profound impact upon international security.  It is true that a very high level of international trade did not prevent the First World War.  However the trade was imperial rather than truly international.  Raw materials were transported up to the imperial states who then turned them into finished products that were sold back to the captive colonial  markets.   Even though trade accounted for approximately 33% of world product, only 11% was between industrialised states. Developed states conducted an arms length exchange of finished manufacturered goods  such as railway engines, ships or  arms.  There was a lot of trade within the imperial blocs but very little between them. 

Trade between industrialised states now accounts for about 65% of the total amount of world trade.  A large proportion of this trade is in components rather than finished manufacturered goods.  In addition to production, firms co-operate in international product development, marketing and finance strategies.  Globalisation has affected all layers of industry.  Leading the trend in globalisation are the worlds 20,000 multinationals that account for some 25-30% of combined GDP in all market economies.  The industries that are most heavily globalised include: motor vehicles; petrochemicals; consumer electronics; tyres; pharmaceuticals; tobacco; soft drinks; fast food; financial consultancies; luxury hotels;  airlines; telecommunications; banking and insurance. Most of the UK's top companies fall in these sectors. 

New optimism

Within the anarchy of international relations the West acts as a bloc of states pursuing interests in common.  The West is a system in which the critical basis for competition is no longer the ownership of military power but economic muscle and the ability to influence ideas.  Within the West there is no longer a need to fight to become the dominant world power. 

The doctrine of mutually assured destruction, which applies to nuclear and modern conventional weapons, assures that no state can expect to gain in absolute terms if it attacks a peer (though there is still plenty  of scope for attacking lesser foes).  The loss of colonial empires has removed an issue that permanently sowed distrust and military competition between the great powers.  During the Cold War the US and the USSR fought out their global ambitions in the Third World.  For the first time under developed states are not the pawns in a global competition played by world governments.  Competition for markets is now economic rather than military. 

UK security

The security of the UK, in military, political and economic terms, lies with the West.  A threat to another member of the West is a threat to our most lucrative markets, the source of components vital to manufacturing goods, investments overseas and the source of inward investment into our economy,  and the stability of world stock, commodity and currency markets.  The freedom of communications that enables free trade  would be compromised if any country in the West faced a military threat. 

Desert Storm showed how the UK's vital interests are held in common with the rest of the Western world.  An international coalition was assembled to free a vital resource that each country, directly or indirectly, depended upon for its survival.  The possession of North Sea oil would  not inure the UK economy from a world wide economic crisis ensuing from Gulf oil supplies being cut. 

As well as showing the strength of the western bloc, Desert Storm showed that while its states normally practiced restraint in relations with each other, they were, and are, prepared to deal ruthlessly with any rival that threatens their interests.  Driving the Iraqi army out of Kuwait helped to maintain international stability.  Should the West ever have to face a much more powerful rival there is the potential for a protracted conflict. 

Strategic realignment

Since the end of the period of idealism after the end of the Cold War,  US relations with China and Russia have worsened.   Both China and Russia are large and well armed enough to be in the first division of powers.  China and Russia pose a potential threat to the West because they both hold values, definitions of the 'national interest', and policies that conflict with the interests and values of the West.  While both states are partially integrated with the global economy, China much more so that Russia, they are not bound to the rest of the world in the way that the truly globalised countries  are.  In addition they resent the power and wealth of western countries and reserve a special enmity to the leader of the West, the USA.  Since the end of the Cold War China and Russia have developed a rapid rapprochement that has the potential to create a rival bloc to the West. 

The problem in the Sino-US relationship is that while China's economy is rapidly becoming internationalised and business interests should be tying her to the western world, politically she has not developed into a member of the West.  China has a marked distaste for democracy, human rights, freedom of movement and international free trade treaties.  More importantly she has used the threat of force to try to bully Taiwan and  her neighbours in the South China Sea.  Western leaders are frequently able to overlook human rights abuses in otherwise friendly states.  However China has broken the entire gamete of political values inherent in the West, she has shown that while she is becoming economically globalised, politically she remains isolated. 

Chinese policy-makers see the world in very different terms to western leaders.  To the decision-makers in Beijing the world is divided into several competing poles, which are the USA, Japan, Russia, Germany/the EU, and China.  These poles are all engaged in a competition for power, influence and ultimately a competition for world domination.  This view is a product  of both Marxist theory which stressed that capitalist states are driven by economic forces to seek world hegemony, and China's history of submission to aggressive European powers during the colonial period. 

For China and Russia  George Bush's 'New World Order' has much more sinister overtones than it does in the West.  The New World Order is seen as a plan to create a world structure that will perpetuate American world domination.  Political reforms have already caused the break-up of the Soviet Union, and calls for reforms in China threaten its own political cohesion.  Chinese leaders fear that the US's insistence upon human rights is part of a secret agenda to make China democratic and therefore weak and fragmented. 

Leaders in Moscow and Beijing are also deeply suspicious of the US world leadership.  The US was able to steamroller world opinion and the structures of the UN in order to mount Desert Storm.  As the only remaining superpower the US is seen as an inevitable rival to the emerging power of China.  A central plank of Chinese foreign policy is therefore to erode America's position as the world's most powerful state. 

China's economic development has not been accompanied by reform at home or political integration with the West.  China has shunned all involvement in regional security and is actively antagonising its neighbours in the South China Sea disputes.  China acts, and perceives her self, much more like a 19th century great power than a modern member of the international community. 

The division of the world

Russians  share China's suspicion of the West and particularly America.  Moves to expand NATO eastwards to involve former Warsaw Pact states are particularly threatening to Moscow.  Economic and political reform, aided and abetted by the West, have resulted in chaos and poverty within Russia and the fragmentation of the Soviet Union. The West is frequently blamed for all of Russia's present day problems.  The 30,000 casualties in Chechnia show that Russia does not show any practice of restraint in dealing with internal opponents to the regime.  While there are profound differences between Russia and China, they both share a hostility toward the West and particularly the USA, a predilection to use military power and a shared history of Marxist animosity to the capitalist democracies. 

Since the late 1980s there has been a steady thaw in relations between Moscow and Beijing.   Since the demise of the Soviet Union the two have become very friendly.  During Defence Minister Pavel Grachev's 1993 visit to Beijing,  Russia and China signed a five-year military co-operation agreement.  Between 1992 and 1994 China spent $2 billion on Russian arms, a figure that rose to $5 billion in 1995 alone.  Advanced missiles, fighter planes and nuclear technology have been bought and  hundreds of Russian scientists work in Beijing's ministry of Aeronautics.  The Chinese navy has been augmented by Russian submarines, and the two countries are even rumoured to be constructing  a new 'stealth missile'. 

The two countries have made moves to patch up long running border disputes.  During the recent crisis over the  Chinese wargames, Russia backed the Chinese claim of sovereignty over Taiwan.  China has tacitly supported Russia's military intervention in Chechnia.  There is a clear rapprochement at work between China and Russia.  This rapprochement is motivated in part by a fear and mistrust of the US and other western states. 

The future

A  long period of friction between the China and the USA is likely.  As long as the US supports Taiwan, and China resents American power and capabilities, Beijing will find excuses to antagonise Washington.  The dilemma for the US lies in whether to confront or integrate with China.  The US could turn a blind eye to Chinese political antagonisms and place her emphasis upon trade and further economic integration in the hope that economic ties would moderate Chinese policy in the long run.  Alternatively she could confront China over issues like human rights, nuclear proliferation and illegal trade practices, and risk totally alienating China from the international system, and losing billions of Chinese export orders.  Until 1996, the US policy was one of integration.  However the Taiwan straits crisis showed that she was willing to change her policy and confront China.  It remains to be seen what her future policy will be. 

In the crisis, Russia and China were lined up against America, while the EU remained silent.  Resentment of American power and arrogance has fuelled Chinese and Russian antagonism.  The Taiwan Straits crisis witnessed the creation of what could loosely be defined as a bloc, Russia and China are edging toward closer co-operation after thirty years of animosity.  We can now talk about the potential for the world being divided into two blocs, China and Russia versus the West lead by America.  This situation is not a return to the Cold War.  The two blocs have considerable trade and cultural links and much to gain from further integration.  However the political unity heralded at the end of the Cold War has ended.  The Taiwan issue showes the future shape of Sino-US relations.  A series of crises rather than outright hostilities is likely.  Nuclear weapons will ensure that the two will not risk full scale war with each other.  The Spratly Islands dispute is a good candidate for the next hot spot. 

The UK and EU will follow the discreet strategy they took in the Taiwan Straits crisis.   By rejecting an overt common foreign policy the EU can avoid taking  a stance in divisive issues, and by remaining silent the EU and act as a vital bridge between Washington, and Moscow and Beijing.  By maintaining a distance from the US the EU may well attract  lucrative export orders away from the American competition.  However ultimately the EU will have to side with the US.  UK and EU interests lie with the West and if there ever was a serious confrontation between the US and China, or even Russia, we would have to fall behind the US, the one remaining superpower and  leading state of the western world. 

Culture and security

Since 1989 the majority of wars have occurred within rather than between states.  National and religious conflicts have replaced wars between as the greatest  threat to international peace and security.  While the potential still exists for wars between the great powers, UK forces are much more likely to be used to clear up the chaos following the collapse of a state like Yugoslavia or Somalia.  All these wars have important local origins, but they are also part of a global trend created by the process of globalisation. 

In 1989 the American Francis Fukuyama predicted that centuries of boredom would follow from the triumph of democracy over all other ideologies.  He believed that the spread of western values like liberal democracy and capitalism would remove ideological conflict and create stable peace loving governments.  The spread of western ideas is part of the process of globalisation.  The whole process is based upon the political and economic freedoms of the market democracy, which have  helped to create stable and pacific regions like Western Europe. 

The spread of  western values like ecumenicalism, democracy, capitalism and the human rights agenda should have eroded the basis for the religious and national militants that hark back to less tolerant times.  Instead globalisation has to take some responsibility for the plethora of civil wars that afflict the world.  Religious and national movements have become more militant and vigorous as a reaction against the onslaught of  globalisation. 

As well as liberal democracy, globalisation is associated with the whole gamete of western culture.  While people in Europe associate it with diversity and the availability of different cultures, the developing world's experience of globalisation is of the import of western food, media and fashions, as well as  western values.  Instead of the diversity of world cultures  found in western cities, the developing world faces the invasion of McDonalds, Hollywood and rock music.  Western culture has been embraced by billions across the globe, however to many other billions it is alien, decadent and immoral. 

Even in the West the global culture has been condemned.  The French fear of the encroachment of English is an example of how the global culture is seen as foreign and unwelcome.  Minority languages are more under threat in the West than the rest of the world as the influences of the dominant culture are stronger.  Similarly there has been a very strong reaction against perceived 'decadence' (especially the acceptance of sexual freedoms) among western conservatives and religious groups. 

Opposing Globalisation - Nationalism and Religion

The reaction against globalisation first became apparent in the advanced industrialised countries whose societies were the most globalised.  During the 1960s and 1970s groups like the Scots in Britain,  Quebecois in Canada, Flemms in Belgium, or Bretons in France  rediscovered a national vitality and asserted themselves on the world stage. The modern resurgence of  national movements in these and most other  Western states can not be explained by resistance to government oppression, the economic or political chaos of the 1930s or persecution from neighbouring nations.  The best explanation is as a reaction to globalisation.  What lay behind the movements was a fear of  traditional languages and customs disappearing in the face of more glamorous foreign imports, and a need to assert a local identity to avoid being lost in the global stage. 

People's local environments are much more important to them than abstract ideas of participating a world stage.  The loss of the traditions and even language of their own communities is frequently much more important to people than the benefits of  access to the international agenda.  Minority groups are parochial.  They have rejected an internationalised way of life to defend their own identity. 

Measures to guarantee regional political autonomy, protect a language and develop some local economic security have become widespread across the western world.  In democracies like Canada or Belgium demands for national autonomy can be peacefully accommodated within the political system.  States like Czechoslovakia have successfully managed a 'divorce', while others have  created a federal structure as a compromise.  Violent conflicts occur when a government or other national group within the state refuses a  demand for autonomy. 

During times of political and economic instability people tend to overestimate the importance of the nation and its ability to provide security and stability.  The revival of national movements in the post-communist world can be partly explained by a desperate need for certainties after countries were stripped of their former ideologies and thrust into the confusion of the global economy and culture.  Nationalists have found security from the dilemmas and upheavals in their new situation in a belief in the nation  and the ability of national unity to protect them. 

Of course national movements existed before they came into contact with globalisation, and there are many other causes of any national revival or conflict.  Self determination is one of the fundamental rights of any people that can reasonably call themselves a nation.   The reaction to globalisation is a new dynamic in the long history of nationalism.  It will ensure that there will be national or ethnic conflicts in the foreseeable future.  As long as globalisation touches every community in the world it will ensure that there will continue to be instabilities as communities assert their right to individuality and some governments attempt to repress a minority rather than give it autonomy. 

The world  revival in both religious and national militancy can not just be explained by economic and political chaos.  Movements in the US, Quebec, the EU or the Gulf  have occurred in some of the most prosperous regions of the world.  While some responsibility can be laid at rising unemployment and economic insecurity (which in its self is a product of the global economy), they are not chronic problems in any of these regions.  Religious and ethnic militancy is a cultural phenomenon that  has a cultural cause. 

The rise in religious fundamentalism is the second destabilising trend to be influenced by globalisation. The Iranian revolution of 1979 was the most dramatic event in what has also become a world trend.  Religious parties have come to power through elections in Turkey and  India, while governments across the Gulf and North Africa  face opposition from militant and popular religious parties.  The growth of fundamentalism is not confined to India and the Middle East.  The USA has seen the rise of  'The New Christian Right',  which has the support of a significant sector of the population and is said to have  influenced both the Regan and Bush presidencies.  The literal interpretation of the bible, which includes the creationist  rejection of  scientific fields like biology, geology, astronomy, and archaeology which for instance do not state that the world was created by God in seven days, can only be described as fundamentalism. 

Religion, like nationalism, is the assertion of an identity.  Though  religion is universal - it transcends cultural and political borders - the modern revival of fundamentalism is almost always in opposition to something.  The rallying cry of Islamic fundamentalism is the opposition to decadent western habits that have corrupted the once 'pure' Islamic society.  In the Middle East religion is the latest reaction to the West.  First  were the national movements that ousted the colonial powers, then came socialist parties aided and abetted by the Soviet Union.  The first two used  ideologies that were developed in the west.  Islam is a  home grown identity that both asserts an extreme form of opposition to the West and is more compatible with traditional values than say socialism. 

The ease of modern communications and the opening of borders have let loose a flood of Western ideas and products across the world.  As they have become predominant Western values have forced traditional religions and cultures to justify themselves on Western terms.  Science and western modes of government, particularly democracy, have questioned faiths and traditions and made them  seem backward and even barbaric. 

Creeds like liberal democracy, human rights and feminism criticize and demand  a complete change in societies.   It is impossible to measure the  extent  that  process of cultural globalisation represents progress, or mere destruction of identities, certainly the developments of the West have brought immeasurable benefits to its own peoples.  What is certain is that many people regard it as something to be opposed. 

The universalisation of Western ideas, and their erosion of faith and traditional society, have forced  difficult choices.  People can either give up their cultures and embrace the new global ethic, or they have to defend their way of lives by embracing the fundamentals of their faiths or ethnic identity.  In many third world countries these choices are seen in the confrontations between a western educated or orientated elite and  traditional  groups that reject 'foreign' ideas. 

Islamic fundamentalists now demand that the 'Umma' be defended from Western ideas like human rights, market democracy and the position of women, ideas that corrupt society.  The supposed decadence of the west has been emphasized by Islamicists and Asian nationalists alike.  Special reference is paid to stories of crime, sexual perversion and drug and alcohol abuse with a disgust that includes a degree of curiosity and fascination.  The same fixation with the decadence of western culture and demands for a return to traditional values can be found in the Christian right in the USA. 

Nationalist groups have had a similar reaction, condemning foreign influences for their erosion of language and other traditions.  Even in the US the consequences of the globalised economy like foreign ownership of industry and  mass migration of immigrants from poorer countries are resented.  Economic insecurity brought on by global competition fans the flames of  far right wing sentiment.   People cling to extreme religious or political ideas in an attempt to gain a sense of meaning and identity within a global culture that makes them seem insignificant. 

The spread of western political ideas has included  the model of the nation state as being the ideal form of government.  For national groups this model creates an imperative to declare independence.  If the only legitimate form of government is the nation state, then  the only legitimate government for an ethnic group is self determined.  The dominance of the nation state as the only form of government has undermined alternatives like multi ethnic states or federations. 

The nation state has also angered religious fundamentalists.  The glorification of the nation denies the legitimacy of other institutions like the church or ultimately God.  The spread of the nation state has been accompanied by the spread of secularised law.  Secularisation of government and particularly education has been very successful in the West.  As it denies the legitimacy of theocratic laws it is in inevitable conflict with religious fundamentalists. 

The last influence of globalisation is the insistence that the world is plural, that there is no superior culture, moral code, or religious message.  The benefits of this plurality is the freedom gained from being able to adopt the lifestyle, food, clothing and religion of one's preference.  Pluralism is however anathema to religious fundamentalism and national chauvinism.  Both religious and national extremists stress that theirs is the one true faith or culture that a people should adhere to. 

Conclusions 

The beginning of the next century will be characterised by continuing tension between the West, and particularly the US, and Russia and China,  bitter local conflicts will threaten the stability of the international order.  Globalisation will be one of the root causes of  both these trends. 

Globalisation has created the West by homogenising the political and economic systems of its members.  The West is a bloc with its own interests and so will attract the jealousy of others.  Both Russia and China share a communist history that  gives them a different outlook and identities to their western neighbours.  That history has ensured that they have become only partially integrated with the world economic and political system.  They have enough contact to create divisive issues, but not enough to bind them to the rest of the developed world. 

The prospect of a return to the Cold War is very distant.  Nuclear weapons will prevent an all out war.  However there will be a series of crises, brinkmanship and possibly limited military engagements in the pursuit of gunboat diplomacy.  Antagonism from China and Russia will severely hinder the international community's ability to deal with regional problems like the collapse of states into civil conflict. 

Local militants asserting their own identity will constitute the greatest threat to the lives and interests of UK nationals.  Extreme groups have, and will continue to use terrorism to further their ends.  Political instability threatens trade and so our own economic security. 

Globalisation has created a period of unprecedented unity and peace between industrialised countries that were once locked into military rivalry.  It has removed the possibility of war with any of the UK's European neighbours.  However globalisation has also brought with it new security challenges that will vex decision-makers in the next century.
